top_choice_rationale: Cărtărescu (P001) best meets my criterion of a voice found in this writer's work and nowhere else, applied to the whole oeuvre within the framework of Nobel's will. On public knowledge, Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid build memory, the body and dream into one cumulative imaginative architecture, and the dense sentences belong to that architecture. The case rests on literary form and sustained imaginative depth, not on nationality, fame or the number of colleagues in agreement. I rank Adonis (P002) second as a serious competitor on merit: renewing the language of a poetic tradition is a weighty achievement, and my discount for him reflects evidentiary confidence about Arabic prosody, not a judgment that he is lesser. Both cases depend on unverified points. For Cărtărescu, I cannot confirm that the very long late books are earned rather than repetitive, or how much Romanian verbal texture survives in translation. Coverage of his poetry, early prose and essays is thin, so a whole-oeuvre citation leans on the major novels. For Adonis, original-language readings are missing, and so is confirmation that the later collections match the early ones. No independent verification of sources is claimed. I prefer either award to no award, since both candidates show distinctive voice, formal ambition and sustained work, so P000 is last.
